content: In adults and children presenting with symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) meningitis, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using the Xpert Ultra test on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as the initial diagnostic tool, rather than relying on smear microscopy or culture methods. Similarly, for individuals with signs of extrapulmonary TB, Xpert Ultra can be used on lymph node aspirates or biopsies as the first diagnostic test for lymph node TB, instead of smear microscopy or culture. Additionally, Xpert Ultra is recommended for detecting rifampicin (RIF) resistance in extrapulmonary TB cases, as it is more effective than culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). For adults with pulmonary TB symptoms and an initial Xpert Ultra trace-positive result, repeated testing with Ultra is not recommended. In children with pulmonary TB symptoms in settings where the pretest probability of TB is less than 5% and the initial Xpert Ultra test is negative, repeated testing with Ultra on sputum or nasopharyngeal aspirates is also not advised. However, in children with a pretest probability of 5% or higher and a negative initial Xpert Ultra result, a second Ultra test (for a total of two tests) may be performed on sputum or nasopharyngeal aspirates. The Truenat MTB, MTB Plus, and MTB-RIF Dx assays utilize chip-based real-time micro PCR technology to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) directly from sputum samples, providing results in under an hour. These assays are designed for use in peripheral laboratories with minimal infrastructure and require only basic technician training. If a positive result is obtained with the MTB or MTB Plus assay, the extracted DNA can be further analyzed using the Truenat MTB-RIF Dx assay to detect mutations associated with RIF resistance. WHO recommends these tests as initial diagnostic tools for pulmonary TB and RIF resistance detection in both adults and children, replacing smear microscopy or culture. The TB-LAMP assay is a manual test that detects MTBC directly from sputum samples within an hour. It does not require advanced instrumentation and can be used in peripheral health centers with biosafety requirements similar to those for sputum-smear microscopy. However, TB-LAMP does not detect resistance to anti-TB drugs. WHO recommends TB-LAMP as a replacement for smear microscopy in diagnosing pulmonary TB in adults with TB symptoms or as a follow-up test for smear-negative specimens. It should not replace molecular tests that detect both MTBC and RIF resistance, especially in populations at risk for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). The urine LF-LAM test detects the mycobacterial lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen in urine and is a potential point-of-care test for certain populations being evaluated for TB. While it lacks sensitivity, it can serve as a rapid bedside rule-in test for HIV-positive individuals, particularly those with advanced HIV disease, serious illness, or low CD4 counts. WHO recommends its use in inpatient settings for HIV-positive adults, adolescents, and children with TB symptoms or advanced HIV disease. In outpatient settings, LF-LAM is suggested for HIV-positive individuals with TB symptoms or low CD4 counts. However, it is not recommended for use in HIV-negative individuals or those without TB symptoms. Low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), such as the Xpert MTB/XDR assay, are designed to detect resistance to isoniazid (INH), fluoroquinolones (FQs), and second-line injectable drugs. These tests are intended for use as follow-up tests in specimens confirmed to be MTBC-positive. WHO recommends their use for detecting resistance to INH and FQs in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases, as well as for detecting resistance to ethionamide (ETO) and amikacin (AMK) in rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) cases. Line probe assays (LPAs) are DNA strip-based tests that detect mutations associated with drug resistance. First-line LPAs (FL-LPAs) can detect resistance to RIF and INH, while second-line LPAs (SL-LPAs) detect resistance to FQs and AMK. WHO recommends FL-LPAs for smear-positive sputum specimens or cultured isolates of MTBC as an initial test for RIF and INH resistance. SL-LPAs are recommended for patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB to detect resistance to FQs and AMK. However, LPAs are not recommended for direct testing of smear-negative specimens. High-complexity reverse hybridization NAATs, such as the GenoScholar PZA-TB test, are used to detect pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance. These tests require culture isolates and are recommended for use in settings with culture facilities. They provide faster results than phenotypic DST but require careful interpretation due to the complexity of the hybridization process. WHO advises against using commercial serologic tests for TB diagnosis due to their inconsistent and imprecise findings, which can lead to false-positive and false-negative results. Additionally, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) should not be used for diagnosing active TB or as part of the diagnostic workup for suspected TB cases. Phenotypic DST remains the reference standard for most anti-TB drugs but is slow and requires specialized infrastructure. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a promising method for rapid detection of drug resistance mutations and may reduce the need for phenotypic DST in patient care and drug-resistant TB surveys.
